beats.title: Code of Hammurabi Sets Penalties
beats.description: A Babylonian king had a table of laws carved in stone, setting fixed punishments for crimes from theft to murder.
beats.note: Sources vary (c. 1772 to 1750 BCE); stele dated c. 1755-1750 BCE

beats.title: Rome Creates the Vigiles
beats.description: Rome's first emperor organised a corps of freedmen to patrol the city's streets, fight fires and catch thieves at night.

beats.title: Newgate Prison Is Built in London
beats.description: A gatehouse in the old city wall became a jail, beginning centuries as London's most notorious prison.
beats.note: Earliest record of a gaol at Newgate

beats.title: Statute of Winchester Sets Watch
beats.description: An English law required towns to post night watchmen and made local men responsible for raising the hue and cry.

beats.title: Bridewell Becomes Correction House
beats.description: A royal palace in London was handed over to hold vagrants and petty offenders and put them to work, a model for later workhouses and prisons.
beats.why_in: origin of the house of correction

beats.title: Paris Gets a Police Chief
beats.description: Louis XIV created a post to oversee the French capital's streets, lighting and order, giving Paris an early organised police.

beats.title: Transportation Act Passed
beats.description: Parliament made shipping convicts to the American colonies a standard punishment, replacing the noose for many offenders.
beats.note: Called the 1717 Act in old-style dating; royal assent March 1718 and first convicts shipped 1718

beats.title: Bow Street Runners Form
beats.description: A London magistrate's small band of paid thief-takers began chasing offenders, an early step toward a professional police.

beats.title: Beccaria Attacks Cruel Punishment
beats.description: An Italian thinker's short book argued against torture and the death penalty and shaped modern ideas of fair punishment.

beats.title: First Fleet Reaches Botany Bay
beats.description: Eleven ships carrying hundreds of convicts arrived in Australia to found Britain's penal colony in New South Wales.

beats.title: Bentham Publishes the Panopticon
beats.description: A philosopher described a circular prison where one watchman could see every inmate, an influential vision of surveillance.

beats.title: First Guillotine Execution
beats.description: A highwayman was beheaded in Paris by a new machine meant to make capital punishment swift and equal.

beats.title: Vidocq Founds the Paris Sûreté
beats.description: A reformed criminal organised a plainclothes brigade that used informers and records to catch thieves, ancestor of modern detective units.

beats.title: Elizabeth Fry Visits Newgate
beats.description: A Quaker reformer began visiting women prisoners in a London jail and campaigned for humane conditions.

beats.title: Auburn Prison Opens
beats.description: A New York prison introduced the system of silent labour by day and solitary cells at night, copied across America.

beats.title: Metropolitan Police Founded
beats.description: Home Secretary Robert Peel launched a uniformed, paid force to patrol London, whose officers became known as bobbies.

beats.title: Scotland Yard Detective Branch
beats.description: London's police formed a small unit of plainclothes officers dedicated to investigating crimes.

beats.title: New York Creates a Uniformed Police
beats.description: The city replaced its night watch with a full-time, paid police department modelled on London's.

beats.title: Pinkerton Agency Founded
beats.description: A Chicago detective opened a private agency whose eye logo gave the world the phrase private eye.

beats.title: Last Public Hanging in England
beats.description: A convicted murderer was hanged outside Newgate, the final execution held before a crowd, after which they moved behind prison walls.

beats.title: Elmira Reformatory Opens
beats.description: A New York prison for young offenders offered schooling, trades and early release for good conduct instead of pure punishment.

beats.title: Bertillon Measures Criminals
beats.description: A Paris police clerk introduced a system of body measurements and photographs to identify repeat offenders.

beats.title: First Electric Chair Execution
beats.description: A New York murderer became the first person put to death by electric current, in a grim trial of a supposedly humane method.

beats.title: Scotland Yard Fingerprint Bureau
beats.description: London's police adopted a filing system for fingerprints, replacing body measurements as the way to identify criminals.

beats.title: FBI Founded
beats.description: The US attorney general created a small corps of special agents that grew into the nation's federal investigative bureau.

beats.title: Wireless Catches Dr Crippen
beats.description: A ship's captain radioed Scotland Yard about a suspicious passenger couple, and a detective overtook them on a faster liner.

beats.title: Polygraph Invented
beats.description: A California police officer and medical student built a device recording blood pressure and breathing to detect lies.

beats.title: Interpol Founded
beats.description: Police chiefs meeting in Vienna set up a commission to help forces in different countries share information on criminals.
beats.note: Founded as the International Criminal Police Commission

beats.title: First Gas Chamber Execution
beats.description: A Nevada prison put a convicted murderer to death with lethal gas, introducing a new method of capital punishment.

beats.title: FBI Opens Its Crime Laboratory
beats.description: The federal bureau set up a central laboratory to analyse evidence such as fingerprints, bullets and fibres for police nationwide.

beats.title: Alcatraz Opens as a Federal Prison
beats.description: An island fortress in San Francisco Bay became a maximum-security prison for the most difficult inmates.

beats.title: 999 Emergency Number Introduced
beats.description: London launched the world's first emergency telephone number so the public could summon police, fire and ambulance help.

beats.title: Britain Ends Hanging for Murder
beats.description: Parliament passed a law suspending the death penalty for murder, first for a trial period and then permanently.

beats.title: Miranda Warning Required
beats.description: A US Supreme Court ruling made police tell suspects they have the right to remain silent before questioning them.

beats.title: First 911 Call Is Made
beats.description: A phone call in a small Alabama town tested a single nationwide emergency number for police, fire and medical help.

beats.title: Crime Stoppers Launches
beats.description: A New Mexico police detective began offering cash rewards for anonymous tips, a scheme later copied around the world.

beats.title: First Lethal Injection Execution
beats.description: A Texas prisoner became the first person executed by intravenous drugs, a method presented as more humane.

beats.title: DNA Fingerprinting Developed
beats.description: A British geneticist found that patterns in DNA could identify individuals, transforming forensic investigation.

beats.title: DNA Evidence Convicts a Killer
beats.description: After mass testing of local men, a baker was convicted of two murders in the first case solved by DNA profiling.
beats.note: Arrested 1987; convicted and sentenced January 1988 (sources agree on 1988)

beats.title: Three Strikes Law Passes
beats.description: California voters and lawmakers imposed life sentences on repeat felons, a model for tough sentencing laws across the US.

beats.title: FBI Automated Fingerprint System
beats.description: A national computer system let police across America search millions of fingerprint records within hours instead of weeks.

beats.title: Golden State Killer Identified
beats.description: Investigators matched crime-scene DNA to relatives on a public ancestry database to arrest a suspect in decades-old cases.
